lines.statement: In adults with a hangover, whether drinking water prevents or relieves it had not been tested in any experimental study up to July 2024, as described in a narrative review (Mackus et al., 2024). In the review authors' own re-analysis of 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who drank more water had worse hangovers, but the amount drunk was not related to how much their hangover or their thirst changed during the day; in student surveys, water was the most used remedy and was rated about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked. After a night of heavy drinking, thirst was clearly raised only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day, and small old studies found mild, short-lived changes in fluid balance, which the authors read as dehydration and hangover being separate effects of drinking. Evidence is insufficient to say whether water helps; the figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Adults with a hangover: 176 walkers in Crete (authors' re-analysis), Dutch students (surveys) and small groups of men in old laboratory studies
lines.exposure: Drinking water during a hangover day (amount self-reported) or as a remedy during or after drinking (survey ratings)
lines.comparator: People who drank less water on the same walk (correlation); no untreated comparison in the surveys
lines.outcome: Hangover severity and thirst ratings and their change during the day; perceived efficacy of water; markers of dehydration
lines.magnitude: Water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk: r = 0.176, 0.243 and 0.229 (p from 0.019 to below 0.001); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst and change in thirst |r| no more than 0.061, none significant. Survey efficacy ratings for water 5.2 to 5.8 out of 10. Thirst above an alcohol-free day only at the 09:30 and 10:30 ratings; hangover above it at every rating to 15:30.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence summarized in a narrative review starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). It complements the later small trial of water during drinking, which found no detectable effect (Imai et al., 2026, a separate claim). The authors' conclusion that water is not effective is not adopted: no trial existed, so the finding is that the question is untested.

lines.q: Is a hangover just being thirsty, and does drinking water fix it?
lines.short: Not just thirst, it seems. Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. No experiment had tested water by mid-2024.
lines.but: It all comes from one review, partly its authors' second look at their own data.
how: Small old studies found mild, brief changes in body fluids after drinking. The review's authors think being dried out and a hangover are separate effects.
Among 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who felt worse drank more water. But drinking more didn't go with getting better faster.
In student surveys, water was the most used hangover remedy. Students gave it about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked.

lines.statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
lines.population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
lines.exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
lines.comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
lines.outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
lines.magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
lines.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.

lines.q: Do habits meant to make drinking less harmful help?
lines.short: Not clearly. Teaching students bundles of habits, like pacing or eating, barely changed their drinking, by their own account. No trial tested one habit alone.
lines.but: Nearly all were US college students. And every result is what they said about themselves.
how: In trials, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They said they drank very slightly less often, and may have had very slightly fewer problems from drinking.
A 2013 review says students reporting more habits nearly always reported drinking less or fewer problems. But most were asked about both at one sitting.
Day by day, students reported drinking more on days with a designated driver or a friend to go home with. The review's author thinks those are planned for heavy nights.

lines.statement: In people who take loperamide to manage opioid withdrawal, evidence is insufficient to say whether loperamide, compared with no loperamide or with withdrawal medicines, relieves withdrawal symptoms: the one study read, a US registry of 26 people seen by medical toxicologists after loperamide exposure (2010 or 2011 to 2016), recorded that 6 of them had taken it to avoid withdrawal, but it recorded only the problems that brought people to care, not whether their withdrawal eased, and it has no comparison group. Its authors write that people use loperamide to relieve withdrawal themselves and that a lack of methadone or buprenorphine treatment may play a part, which the study did not measure. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who take loperamide to avoid or relieve opioid withdrawal (6 of 26 registry cases seen by US medical toxicologists)
lines.comparator: No loperamide, or withdrawal medicines (no data)
lines.magnitude: No data: relief of withdrawal was not recorded. 6 of the 12 misuse cases (26 in all) had taken loperamide to avoid withdrawal; their outcomes are not reported separately.
lines.reasoning: No study read measured whether loperamide relieves opioid withdrawal; the only source records why 6 people took it and the harms seen in those who reached a toxicologist. Observational, so it starts low; indirectness -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The claim states that the question is untested in what was read, not that loperamide does not work.

lines.q: Does loperamide help with opioid withdrawal?
lines.short: We can't say. The one study we read didn't check if loperamide eased opioid withdrawal.
lines.but: It only counted people who saw a poisons doctor. And it had no group to compare them with.
how: A US registry counted 26 people seen by poisons doctors after taking loperamide. Six of them took it to avoid withdrawal.
It recorded the problems that brought people to care, not whether their withdrawal eased.
The authors think a lack of methadone or buprenorphine treatment may be part of why people take it for withdrawal. The study didn't measure that.

lines.statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm as an outcome of a practice. Practices appear as people's accounts, researchers' recommendations and reports of behaviour after drug checking: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, in a qualitative study) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. Numbers come only from two drug-checking studies, and they describe behaviour, not harm: in a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips, 69% of the 68 followed up a month later reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%; and in an observational study of 541 adults who use drugs in several US states, a positive fentanyl test-strip result went, over 28 days, with reports of using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (an association in the review's table, which its text words as a result of the strip). The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, qualitative, ethnographic, survey, pilot and observational sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore; 541 adults who use drugs in several US states
lines.exposure: Practices people use themselves before or during use, as described: limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they use, avoiding alcohol at the same time, comparing vendors and batches, peer check-ins, not using or injecting alone; and reported behaviour after a test-strip result (asking someone to check on them, using smaller amounts, taking turns, keeping naloxone nearby)
lines.comparator: None: no source compared people using a practice with people not using it; the two test-strip studies compared reports before and after receiving strips, or related behaviour to the strip result
lines.outcome: Any harm, such as overdose, assault, injury or arrest (not measured against a comparison in any source); reported behaviour after a test-strip result
lines.magnitude: No source compared people who used a practice with people who did not, and none measured harm. Behaviour after test strips: in a before-and-after pilot (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result; in an observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result went with using smaller amounts, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, most strongly when benzodiazepines were tested (sizes given only in the review's table, second-hand).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive and qualitative sources start low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a scoping review, a narrative synthesis without appraisal, so it stays at draft and its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). That no practice has been tested is itself the finding (decision p-before-during-after); section 7, findings only, held for the senior author. Status single study: one review.

lines.q: Do people's own habits lower the harms of benzos?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet. A 2025 review of benzo harm reduction found no study that checked whether any habit lowers harm.
lines.but: It's what people said and what researchers suggest, from one review. It didn't check how good its sources were.
how: People on a Swedish forum about flubromazolam, a newer benzo, wrote of staying home. They also wrote of keeping it out of reach while high, and not drinking with it.
In Canada, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs set up friend groups to check on each other. They feared benzos in their drugs, and sexual assault.
People whose test strip found fentanyl reported taking more care, like keeping naloxone nearby. That's a medicine for opioid overdose. The link was strongest when they tested benzos.

lines.statement: In adults who have used classic psychedelics, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything people do during a difficult experience makes it shorter or easier: no study read here tested a way of coping, and what is known is what people say helped, looking back. Two independent surveys agree only that a calming or accepting response (trying to calm the mind; letting go or accepting the experience) was the one most often named as helpful; their lists and questions differed, so their percentages cannot be compared. In a self-selected online survey of 529 people recalling a challenging experience with a classic psychedelic or an analogue (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; use combined with non-classic drugs such as MDMA or ketamine was allowed) (Wood et al., 2024), the responses, of 26 listed, most often tried and judged helpful were letting go, accepting or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%); the least often were directing anger at the experience (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling it to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%). People who judged more of the 11 responses that the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal helpful rated their emotional breakthrough higher (r = 0.50), but that group also includes breathing, closing the eyes, questioning the experience, telling it to stop and directing anger at it; both were rated at one sitting, sometimes years later, and judging a response helpful may itself reflect how the experience ended. Sixteen people who had attended psilocybin retreats, chosen because their difficult ceremonies had been followed by personal change, wrote of breathing on purpose, opening their eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, and facilitators' touch, listening, reassurance and reminders to breathe, among other responses. In a US online panel, 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience, ticked what had helped during their most challenging one: trying to calm the mind 257 (41.9%), changing location 168 (27.4%), asking a friend for help 124 (20.2%), changing the people around 124 (20.2%), smoking cannabis 113 (18.4%) and changing the music 99 (16.2%); fewer ticked drinking alcohol (54, 8.8%) or taking another drug (22, 3.6%) (Simonsson et al., 2023). No study tested any of these responses, including taking cannabis, alcohol or another drug, which in the other survey was among the responses least often judged helpful (12.1%). As summarized second-hand in a mini review (Piercey et al., 2024), 91% of respondents to an earlier survey of difficult experiences with psilocybin mushrooms used at least one such strategy and rated them only modestly effective, and 65.9% of surveyed callers to a psychedelic peer-support phone line (the drugs they had taken are not stated) said it helped ease their distress. None of these studies compared people who did something with people who did not. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults who have used classic psychedelics and recalled a challenging experience: a self-selected online sample (529), retreat attendees chosen for personal change after difficult ceremonies (16) and a US online panel (613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience)
lines.exposure: Responses during a challenging experience (accepting, observing, lying down, calming the mind, changing place, people or music, asking for help, taking another drug), as respondents recalled them and judged their helpfulness
lines.comparator: None: no comparison of people who used a response with people who did not
lines.outcome: Self-judged helpfulness during the experience; emotional breakthrough rated afterwards (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory)
lines.magnitude: No effect estimates. Tried and judged helpful (Wood et al., 2024; n = 529): letting go 84.5%, observing the mind 77.3%, closing the eyes or lying down 73.9%; least often anger 9.4%, trying to sleep 9.7%, telling it to stop 10.6%, another drug or alcohol 12.1%. Count of the 11 responses grouped as acceptance and reappraisal judged helpful, against emotional breakthrough rated at the same sitting: r = 0.50. Ticked as helpful (Simonsson et al., 2023; n = 613, including 362 who said they had never had a challenging experience): calming the mind 41.9%, changing location 27.4%, asking a friend 20.2%, changing the people around 20.2%, cannabis 18.4%, changing the music 16.2%, alcohol 8.8%, another drug 3.6%. The two surveys' percentages are not comparable (different lists, questions and denominators). Second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024): 91% used strategies, rated modestly effective; 65.9% of helpline callers found it helpful.
lines.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated refers to the reports only: two independent surveys (University College London; a Karolinska, Oxford and Wisconsin team), with different lists and questions, agree that a calming or accepting response was the one most often named as helpful; no study tested whether any response works. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.

lines.q: What helps people get through a difficult psychedelic trip?
lines.short: Looking back, people most often say letting go or calming the mind helped them through a hard psychedelic trip. None of it was tested.
lines.but: These are memories, sometimes years old, from people who chose to answer. Saying something helped may just reflect how the trip ended.
how: In an online survey, 529 people recalled a hard trip on a classic psychedelic, like psilocybin or LSD. 85 in 100 had tried letting go and found it helpful.
Least often tried and found helpful were getting angry at it and trying to sleep. Taking another drug or a drink was near the bottom too.
In a US survey, trying to calm the mind was ticked as helpful most often. Next came changing place and asking a friend for help.

lines.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy, evidence is insufficient to say whether harm reduction habits lower the chance of a difficult experience. The one survey read here that measured both (Palmer and Maynard, 2022; pre-registered) asked 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people (median 11.5 lifetime uses), reached through university societies and online psychedelic communities, to recall their first experience (a median of 42 months earlier) and their most recent one (a median of 2 months earlier): which listed practices they had used before, during and after, how challenging it had been (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) and how much emotional breakthrough it brought (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory). A score adding up the practices each person used, each weighted by how important the sample rated it for safety, correlated weakly with lower challenge for the first experience (r = −0.21, 95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) and not significantly for the most recent (r = −0.15, −0.30 to 0.00), and with more breakthrough on both occasions (r = 0.24, 0.09 to 0.38), 2 to 6% of the variation (editors' intervals and calculation). The score counted practices after the experience, which cannot have shaped it, was weighted by the respondents' own judgments, was recalled at the same sitting as the outcomes and was not adjusted for anything, and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. Scores were higher for the most recent experience (48.7 against 40.1), for practices before and after use but not during it, while challenge scores were about the same (17.1 and 17.3% of the maximum). Most were with trusted friends, a practice the sample rated important; few had a sober sitter, which it rated low; and few tested their drugs, although testing was rated important. In a US online panel, 182 of 613 people (29.7%) linked their most challenging experience to having had no preparation; that link went with slightly higher challenge ratings for the same experience, rated at the same sitting (standardized beta 0.09), but not with later thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others (adjusted odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.45) (Simonsson et al., 2023). A mini review that relies heavily on the first survey for its outcome evidence summarizes it as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, which overstates it (the score was weighted, and the link with challenge held for the first experience only); the review adds a catalogue of strategies named in the literature and finds outcome research scarce: besides that survey, one preparedness-scale study of psychedelic use (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and, for MDMA, a rapid scoping review whose reference is a preprint, all second-hand (Piercey et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who use classic psychedelics outside research or therapy: a self-selected survey of experienced people (163) and a US online panel (613); a mini review of the literature
lines.exposure: Harm reduction practices before, during and after use, recalled and weighted by importance; having had no preparation, as a respondent's own explanation of their most challenging experience
lines.comparator: People who recalled fewer or less highly rated practices; respondents who did not link their most challenging experience to having had no preparation
lines.outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), emotional breakthrough (Emotional Breakthrough Inventory), thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others
lines.magnitude: Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163: importance-weighted practice score and challenge r = −0.21 (95% CI −0.35 to −0.06) for the first experience, −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00) for the most recent; with breakthrough r = 0.24 (0.09 to 0.38) on both (editors' intervals; 2% to 6% of the variation). Score 40.06 first against 48.68 most recent; challenge 17.14 against 17.29 per cent of the maximum. Simonsson et al. (2023): no preparation linked to the most challenging experience by 182 of 613; challenge standardized beta 0.09; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others adjusted OR 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45).
lines.reasoning: Cross-sectional self-report starts low; down two for risk of bias, giving very low. Status single study: the habits-experience association rests on one survey; the panel survey's item is a different measure (an attribution of the worst experience), and the review adds no primary data and misreports the survey, so it is cited only for what it adds. Section 7 (decision p-before-during-after): findings only, for the senior author's approval.

lines.q: Do harm reduction habits mean fewer difficult psychedelic trips?
lines.short: Nobody can say yet. In one survey, a higher score for safety habits went with a slightly easier first psychedelic trip. Not clearly the latest, though.
lines.but: People recalled habits and trips at one sitting, often years later. And people who quit after a hard first trip couldn't take part.
how: 163 experienced people, mostly men, recalled their first and latest trip. They said which safety habits they'd used and how hard each trip was.
A higher habit score also went with more emotional breakthrough on both trips. All these links were weak.
Most were with trusted friends. Few had a sober sitter or tested their drugs, though the group rated testing as important.
In a US survey, 30 in 100 people linked their hardest trip to having had no preparation. They rated that trip slightly harder.

lines.statement: In people diagnosed with eye damage after using poppers (113 people in 32 published reports, 2004 to 2021, pooled in a systematic review), evidence is insufficient to say whether stopping poppers, or taking lutein supplements, compared with continuing or not taking them, helps vision recover: treatment was documented for 45 people, of whom 42 were advised to stop (3 of them also given lutein) and 2 were given lutein alone; whether people really stopped was recorded for 27 (19 had); there was no comparison group, and the review states that the effect of treatment or of stopping on vision could not be analysed. Scans improved in most of those followed up (46 of 75), but this cannot be tied to stopping: of the two people followed longest, one who reportedly kept using had unchanged vision and one whose stopping was not recorded improved, and some earlier series saw no improvement in the first months despite stopping. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People diagnosed with eye damage after poppers use (113 published cases, 2004 to 2021)
lines.exposure: Stopping poppers use, or oral lutein
lines.comparator: Continuing use, or no lutein (no comparison group in the reports)
lines.outcome: Recovery of vision and of retinal findings
lines.magnitude: No comparative data. Stopping advised for 42 of the 45 with treatment documented; lutein for 5 (3 with stopping, 2 alone); compliance recorded for 27 (19 compliant); OCT improved or resolved in 46 of 75 followed up, without data by stopping.
lines.reasoning: Observational case data start low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Stopping poppers and lutein are what people with this diagnosis were told to do, but no report compared them with not doing so; the improvement seen in many followed-up cases may be the natural course. The claim states findings only (section 7).

lines.q: If poppers hurt my eyes, does stopping them or lutein help?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet, for either. Eye scans improved in 46 of 75 people checked again, but no report compared stopping poppers with carrying on.
lines.but: These are case reports with no comparison group. Whether people really stopped was recorded for only 27 of 113.
how: In a review of case reports, almost everyone whose treatment was recorded was told to stop poppers. Whether stopping helped vision couldn't be analysed.
Of the two followed longest, the one said to have kept using had no change in vision. The other improved, but nobody recorded whether they'd stopped.
Some earlier reports saw no improvement in the first months, even in people who stopped.
Lutein, a supplement, went to only 5 people, with nobody to compare them with.

lines.statement: In people with constipation caused by opioids, evidence from the sources read is insufficient to say whether over-the-counter laxatives, compared with placebo or with prescription medicines, relieve it: a meta-analysis of 27 placebo-controlled trials of prescription medicines (searched to March 2017) included no trial of an over-the-counter laxative, and its authors write that such laxatives are often tried first, that their effect in opioid-induced constipation is hard to assess from existing studies because of varied methods, missing data and risk of bias (citing two Cochrane reviews of laxatives in palliative care, not read for this claim), and that prescription laxatives may not be better than over-the-counter ones. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People with opioid-induced constipation (the review's trials were mostly in people taking opioids for chronic pain)
lines.comparator: Placebo, or prescription medicines for opioid-induced constipation
lines.magnitude: No data in the review read: no over-the-counter laxative trial was included. The authors' remark that their effect is hard to assess cites two Cochrane reviews in palliative care (Candy et al. 2011 and 2015), not read.
lines.reasoning: The question matters in real life (ordinary laxatives are what most people try first), but the sources read hold no data on it: the meta-analysis did not include such laxatives, and its authors' remark is second-hand. Starting low because no randomized evidence on the question was read; indirectness -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The Cochrane review the authors cite (Candy et al. 2015, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD003448.pub4) is the source to read next.

lines.q: Do ordinary laxatives from the shop help constipation caused by opioids?
lines.short: We can't say yet. The one review we read on opioid constipation had no trials of laxatives from the shop.
lines.but: What we read has no data on it, only its authors' remarks. One of them rests on two reviews we haven't read.
how: The review pooled trials of prescription medicines only. Its authors write that people often try shop laxatives first.
But they say the studies so far make the effect of shop laxatives hard to judge.
They also write that prescription laxatives may not work better than shop ones. They didn't test this.

lines.statement: In children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD who were taking stimulant medicine and took more than an hour to fall asleep (27 or 28 children in the run-in phase of a trial in a Vancouver hospital ADHD programme; Weiss et al., 2006), a sleep-routine programme (a regular bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, worked out with parents from sleep diaries), compared with the same children's sleep before it, is associated with falling asleep sooner: from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on parents' diaries and from 98.1 to 73.0 minutes on wrist activity monitors (effect size 0.67), with less variation from night to night on the diaries. Only 5 children then fell asleep within an hour, clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved and 54% unchanged, and ADHD ratings did not change. There was no comparison group, so part of the change may have happened anyway, for example because children were chosen when their sleep was at its worst. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Children aged 6 to 14 with ADHD on stable stimulant medicine taking more than 60 minutes to fall asleep, in a hospital ADHD programme
lines.exposure: A sleep-hygiene programme: a consistent bedtime and waking time, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from sleep diaries (study conditions in the study card)
lines.comparator: The same children's sleep in the nights before the programme (no control group)
lines.outcome: Time to fall asleep (parent diaries and actigraphy), night-to-night variability, clinician-rated improvement, ADHD symptoms
lines.magnitude: Sleep-onset latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; 5 children below 60 minutes; clinicians: 21% much or very much improved, 54% unchanged.
lines.reasoning: An uncontrolled before-after comparison starts low; risk of bias −1 gives very low. Status single study.

lines.q: Do bedtime routines help children on ADHD stimulants fall asleep?
lines.short: Maybe a little. With a set routine, children on ADHD stimulants fell asleep in 69 minutes on average, down from 92. Most still took at least an hour.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, so part of the change may have happened anyway. For example, children were picked when their sleep was at its worst.
how: The children were 6 to 14 and took over an hour to fall asleep. The routine meant regular bed and wake times, no caffeine and no naps.
Wrist monitors showed a similar drop. But only 5 of about 28 children then fell asleep within an hour.
Clinicians rated 21 in 100 children much or very much better and 54 in 100 unchanged. ADHD ratings didn't change.
